BEFORE THE STATION HOUSE OFFICER / OFFICER IN CHARGE,
[NAME OF POLICE STATION], [DISTRICT], [STATE]

COMPLAINT / WRITTEN INFORMATION OF A COGNIZABLE OFFENCE UNDER SECTION 154 OF THE CODE OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE, 1973
(Offence: causing death by a rash and negligent act, Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860)

Date: 20 June 2024

COMPLAINANT: [NAME, PARENTAGE, AGE, OCCUPATION AND ADDRESS OF THE COMPLAINANT], [RELATIONSHIP TO THE DECEASED]

ACCUSED: [NAME AND ADDRESS OF THE ACCUSED, OR "UNKNOWN PERSON" IF NOT KNOWN]

To,
The Station House Officer,
[NAME OF POLICE STATION]

Sir,

The complainant respectfully submits as follows:

A. FACTS

1. The complainant is [DESCRIPTION OF THE COMPLAINANT AND RELATIONSHIP WITH THE DECEASED, [NAME OF THE DECEASED]].

2. On 1 February 2024, at about [TIME], at [PLACE OF INCIDENT, WITHIN THE LIMITS OF THIS POLICE STATION], [NAME OF THE DECEASED] died as a result of an act done by the accused, [NAME OF THE ACCUSED].

3. [DESCRIBE THE RASH AND NEGLIGENT ACT OF THE ACCUSED: THE VEHICLE, MACHINE OR ACTIVITY INVOLVED, THE MANNER IN WHICH IT WAS DRIVEN OR HANDLED, AND HOW THE DEATH FOLLOWED FROM IT].

4. The death was the direct result of the rash and negligent act of the accused. The accused neither intended to cause death nor knew that the act would in all probability cause death. [PARTICULARS OF EYEWITNESSES, MEDICAL TREATMENT, INQUEST OR POST-MORTEM, IF ANY].

5. The complainant approached the police on 20 June 2024, which is after the incident. [REASONS FOR THE INTERVAL BETWEEN 1 FEBRUARY 2024 AND 20 JUNE 2024, IF ANY]. A delay in lodging information does not by itself take the matter outside the duty to register and investigate a cognizable offence.

B. THE OFFENCE AND THE APPLICABLE LAW

6. Penal section. The incident occurred on 1 February 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. The offence is therefore governed by the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves for offences committed before that date. Article 20(1) of the Constitution also forbids punishing an act under a law that was not in force when it was done. The accused is to be charged under **Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** [corresponding to Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, cited only as the new equivalent].

7. The Supreme Court has held, in *Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab* ([AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED]; the passage is quoted at paragraph 17 of the Bombay High Court's decision in BA/838/2025, *Vishal alias Uddhav Dnyaneshwar Chavan v. State of Maharashtra* (2025), and the Supreme Court report is to be verified), that Section 304A applies where there is no intention to cause death and no knowledge that the act will in all probability cause death. The section applies only to acts that are rash or negligent and are directly the cause of death. Whether the conduct was culpably rash or negligent depends on the care and circumspection that a prudent and reasonable person would consider sufficient in the circumstances of each case. In *Shankar Narayan Bhadolkar v. State of Maharashtra* ([AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED]; the passage is quoted at paragraph 18 of the Bombay High Court's decision in BA/838/2025, *Vishal alias Uddhav Dnyaneshwar Chavan v. State of Maharashtra* (2025), and the Supreme Court report is to be verified), the Supreme Court held that where intention or knowledge is the motivating force of the act, Section 304A must give way to the graver charge of culpable homicide. On the facts stated above there was neither intention nor knowledge, so Section 304A is the appropriate section.

8. Procedural section. The proceeding began on 20 June 2024, which is before 1 July 2024, so it was pending immediately before that date. Under section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, it continues under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [and, for evidence, under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 by section 170(2) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023]. Accordingly:

(a) This information is to be registered as a First Information Report under **Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973** [Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, cited only as the new equivalent]. Section 154(1) requires every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence to be reduced to writing, signed by the informant, and entered in the prescribed book.

(b) The case is to be investigated under **Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973** [Section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, cited only as the new equivalent]. Under Section 157(1), the officer in charge, having reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence that he is empowered to investigate, must forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance and must proceed to the spot, or depute a subordinate officer to do so. The proviso to Section 157(1) permits non-investigation only where the case is not serious or there is no sufficient ground, and neither condition applies here, as a death has occurred.

C. PRAYER

The complainant therefore prays that the Station House Officer may be pleased to:

(i) register this information as a First Information Report under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for the offence under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and supply a free copy to the complainant;

(ii) investigate the case under Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and send the report to the Magistrate forthwith;

(iii) visit the spot, record the statements of witnesses, and collect the medical, inquest and other material evidence;

(iv) arrest the accused, if necessary, and file a report on completion of the investigation against [NAME OF THE ACCUSED] under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; and

(v) pass such other orders as may be just.

D. VERIFICATION

I, [NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], declare that the contents of paragraphs 1 to 5 are true to my knowledge and that I have suppressed nothing material. Paragraphs 6 to 8 are submitted on legal advice.

Date: 20 June 2024

**[NAME OF THE ACCUSED]**, aged [AGE], resident of [ADDRESS] ... **Accused**

Date of the complaint: [DATE]. The complainant first approached the police on 15 January 2025.

To,
The Station House Officer, [NAME OF POLICE STATION]

Sir,

The complainant respectfully states as follows:

**A. FACTS**

1. The complainant is a woman residing at [ADDRESS]. The accused is [RELATIONSHIP / ACQUAINTANCE OF THE ACCUSED WITH THE COMPLAINANT, AND POSITION OF TRUST OR AUTHORITY, IF ANY].

2. From 10 January 2023 to 31 December 2024 the accused assaulted the complainant and used criminal force against her, intending to outrage her modesty or knowing it to be likely that he would thereby outrage it.

3. The particulars of the acts are: [DESCRIPTION OF EACH ACT, WITH DATE, TIME AND PLACE, TO BE SUPPLIED FROM THE COMPLAINANT'S INSTRUCTIONS]. The witnesses, if any, are [NAMES OF WITNESSES].

4. The conduct complained of is one continuing course of conduct. It began before 1 July 2024, was not interrupted, and continued after that date until 31 December 2024.

5. The complainant approached the police on 15 January 2025. [REASONS FOR THE INTERVAL BETWEEN THE LAST ACT AND THE COMPLAINT, IF ANY.]

6. The complainant has not previously lodged any complaint or information about these acts [OR: DETAILS OF EARLIER COMPLAINTS, IF ANY].

**B. THE PENAL PROVISION UNDER WHICH THE ACCUSED IS TO BE CHARGED**

7. *The offence.* The offence is assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty. Under the repealed Indian Penal Code, 1860 this was section 354, which punished whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty. Its equivalent in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is **section 74**.

8. *Continuing offence, charged once.* On the complainant's case the conduct is one continuing offence, not a series of separate offences. A continuing offence is one susceptible of continuance, as distinguished from one committed once and for all. [AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED, FROM THE SUPREME COURT, ON CONTINUING OFFENCES. The formulation is drawn from State of Bihar v. Deokaran Nenshi, as quoted in the Gujarat High Court's decision in Jafar Abbas Rasoolmohammad Merchant v. State of Gujarat (2015); that is a single-bench High Court decision and is not binding authority for this proposition, so the Supreme Court decision itself should be cited and verified before filing.]

9. *Code applicable.* The conduct ran across 1 July 2024 and was still being committed after it. It is therefore charged once, and not split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge. Section 9(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita permits one punishment for an offence made up of parts. Under section 1(3) of the Sanhita, liability for an offence still being committed after the commencement date is under the Sanhita. Section 518 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita treats a continuing offence as running afresh at every moment of its continuance.

10. *Section for the charge.* The accused is accordingly to be charged **once, under section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** [corresponding to section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860]. If the Investigating Officer or the Court finds that the acts were separate offences, each complete when done, each is to be charged under the code in force on the day it was done. Acts before 1 July 2024 would then be charged under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (saved by section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita), and acts on or after that date under section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

11. [IF THE ACCUSED STANDS IN A POSITION OF TRUST OR AUTHORITY: ANY ENHANCED PUNISHMENT APPLICABLE TO BE CHECKED AGAINST THE ENACTED TEXT OF SECTION 74 OF THE BNS AND ANY STATE AMENDMENT.]

**C. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISIONS UNDER WHICH THE CASE IS TO BE REGISTERED AND INVESTIGATED**

12. *Registration.* This proceeding began on 15 January 2025, after 1 July 2024. Nothing in it was pending immediately before that date, so section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which saves the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, does not apply. The date of the offence does not enter that test. The information is therefore to be registered as an FIR under **section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)]. The text of section 173 is not set out here. The corresponding section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had a proviso requiring that information from a woman against whom an offence under section 354 of the Indian Penal Code is alleged be recorded by a woman police officer. The complainant requests that her statement be recorded by a woman police officer [ADVOCATE TO CONFIRM THE CORRESPONDING PROVISION OF SECTION 173 OF THE BNSS].

13. *Investigation.* The investigation is to proceed under **section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [section 157, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (repealed)]. Under section 176(1), an officer in charge who has reason to suspect the commission of an offence he is empowered to investigate must forthwith send a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance. He must then proceed in person, or depute a subordinate officer, to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances and, if necessary, take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender. The proviso to section 176(1) and section 176(2) require reasons to be recorded if he does not so proceed, and require the informant to be notified if he declines to investigate.

14. *Evidence.* Evidence in the case is governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, because the proceeding began after 1 July 2024.

**D. PRAYER**

The complainant prays that the Station House Officer may be pleased to:

(a) register an FIR on this complaint under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 for the offence under section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [section 354, Indian Penal Code, 1860];
(b) investigate under section 176 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, and send the report to the Magistrate;
(c) have the complainant's statement recorded by a woman police officer, and furnish her a copy of the FIR free of cost; and
(d) pass such other orders as are just.

**VERIFICATION**

I, [NAME OF THE COMPLAINANT], state that the contents of paragraphs 1 to 6 are true to my knowledge, and that the rest are based on legal advice believed by me to be correct. Nothing material has been concealed.

Place: [PLACE]  Date: [DATE]

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE. You have asked for submissions that a Transfer of Property Act tenancy dispute is not arbitrable, built on Himangni. The first step is to tell you plainly that the sources show this proposition is no longer good law as a general rule, and that the argument cannot responsibly be built as framed.

LAW AND COURT POSITION. Himangni, as quoted in the Delhi High Court extract [6], held that where the rent statute is inapplicable the parties' rights are governed by the Transfer of Property Act, so that a civil suit and not arbitration is the forum. [UNVERIFIED AS BINDING — this proposition tracks a non-binding opinion in the cited case] Section 105 of the Act [1] and s. 8 of the Arbitration Act [3] do not themselves say that. Section 8 requires reference unless prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists. Vidya Drolia (2019) [8] records, in the headnote, that Himangni noticed none of the Transfer of Property Act provisions, that the Act is silent on arbitrability, and that the case requires a relook by three Judges. The 2025 Delhi order [7] quotes a Supreme Court passage stating that Himangni's ratio is overruled and that landlord-tenant disputes are arbitrable because the Transfer of Property Act does not forbid arbitration. The same passage excludes disputes governed by rent control legislation where a specific court or forum has exclusive jurisdiction. I am treating that quotation as the overruling, but the extract does not name the judgment. Its bench strength, date and citation must be confirmed from the certified copy before you tell the Court anything about it. Under Article 141 the overruling decision binds you, and any citation of Himangni as good law without disclosing it would be a serious professional risk.

APPLICATION. The submissions still open depend on the facts, which you have not given me. If the premises fall under a rent control statute that vests exclusive jurisdiction in a specified court or forum, you can invoke the carve-out preserved in the quoted passage [7] and Booz Allen as summarised in Vidya Drolia [8]. That carve-out requires a special statute, statutory protection against eviction for the tenant, and exclusive jurisdiction in a specified court. Each limb must be shown on the statute. If the claim is about whether a lease was validly determined, note that the headnote [8] treats that as something an arbitrator can decide. A further argument is that the arbitration agreement does not exist or does not cover the dispute, for example where the lease expired and the tenant holds over without a written agreement. That is the reading of Himangni put in Rani Suri [6], but that passage is non-binding and the point is one of fact. Section 8 [3] also permits the prima facie 'no valid agreement' objection, and Yashpal & Sons [5] shows that execution authority and consideration are left to the arbitrator at the appointment stage.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The respondent will cite the overruling and the Delhi decisions [5][7], and will say that s. 16 and s. 34(2)(b) [4] provide the safety valves. The Delhi High Court in Reema Singal [7] sent the arbitrability objection to the tribunal under s. 16, and that is a likely outcome of any appointment challenge. Our strongest counter is the statutory forum carve-out, which defeats the opposing case only where the statute actually applies to these premises. Citing Himangni without disclosure risks a loss of credibility.

LIMITS. The sources do not contain the text of Himangni or of the overruling judgment. They do not identify which rent statute applies to your client's premises, and I have invented no facts about the lease, the parties or the forum.

The headnote records the Court setting aside the bail denials and remanding them 'without application of the twin conditions' [2]. The ratio, on the material before me, turned on the structure of the pre-2018 provision: the conditions attached only to offences punishable with more than three years under Part A of the Schedule, so that similar offenders received different bail outcomes depending on whether s. 45 applied [2][3]. The Punjab and Haryana decision [5] reads the judgment as also relying on the anticipatory-bail anomaly. The excerpts do not let me confirm each ground of the ratio, so check paras 26-31 and 45 of the official report.

The 2018 amendment replaced the Part A reference with 'under this Act' and added the Rs one crore proviso [1][4]. The High Court excerpts record the ED's argument that this cured the defect [3][4]. If, as your instructions state, Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (2022) 9 SCC 1 [CITATION UNVERIFIED] upheld the amended conditions as constitutional, that holding binds every court under Art 141 and, being later, post-dates Nikesh. The Supreme Court is not bound by a co-ordinate or smaller bench, but a division bench cannot depart from a larger bench. Vijay Madanlal is not in the sources and I cannot describe its reasoning.

1. Frame the case as one on the pre-amendment provision. 2. Confine the argument to application, not validity. Rely on the provisos in s. 45(1) (woman, sick or infirm, under sixteen, less than Rs one crore) if the facts fit [1].
3. Preserve a reasoned challenge for a larger bench only if you can identify a ground Vijay Madanlal did not decide. The sources do not identify one.
4. Use the anomaly reasoning [5] as persuasive material on arbitrariness under Art 14, noting it is an NDPS decision.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The Union will say the 2018 amendment removed the Part A classification that led to Nikesh Tarachand Shah, that Vijay Madanlal upheld the amended text, and that any contrary submission is barred by Art 141. This would be strong, and it is defeated only if the offence pre-dates the amendment or the point you raise was not decided in Vijay Madanlal.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: Whether the State can impose, on private unaided institutions, a scheme that fixes fees or shares seats.

LAW: Article 19(1)(g) and Article 30(1) protect the right to establish and administer institutions. Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6) permit regulation in the public interest.

COURT POSITION: The foundation is T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002, 11 judges). On the extracts in the sources, it permits regulation to maintain academic standards and prevent maladministration, treats a rigid fee structure as unacceptable, and allows merit-based admissions with a prescribed management percentage [4]. Islamic Academy [1] affirmed maximum autonomy for unaided institutions, including minority ones, in recruitment, fees and admissions. It also noted that the Unni Krishnan scheme, which nationalised education, was unconstitutional. Its own scheme of quota sharing and fee committees was then disapproved by P.A. Inamdar (7 judges), which held that States cannot fix seat-sharing quotas in unaided institutions and that local needs are no ground [4]. Because Inamdar is a larger bench than Islamic Academy and the later decision, that part of Islamic Academy is not good law; only its autonomy statements remain usable. On fees, Indian School, Jodhpur [3], relying on the Constitution Bench in Modern Dental College, holds that management may devise its fee structure, but commercialisation and capitation fee are impermissible. The Government may regulate at the initial stage, and may direct reduction of excessive fees. A reasonable surplus for growth and development is a recognised cost component [3].

APPLICATION: A challenge to a statute or order that fixes fee rates, or reserves a share of seats for the State in an unaided school or college, would rely on Inamdar and Pai Foundation. The State will rely on Indian School, Jodhpur and Modern Dental College and say that the measure only prevents profiteering. The deciding question is therefore whether the scheme leaves the institution its own fee structure and a reasonable surplus, or substitutes the State's fee and seat allocation. Karnataka's experience [2] shows the autonomy argument succeeding against Section 48 of the Karnataka Education Act, although the excerpt does not show the final disposition.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will argue that autonomy is not absolute [3], that fee regulation is an anti-commercialisation measure, and that Indian School, Jodhpur is a later decision. The answer is that it regulates only the manner of fixing fees and does not restore a quota scheme, and that the seat-quota holding of Inamdar is untouched. For education-related quotas by statute, for example reservations under Article 15(5), the sources do not address the position, and it must be separately checked.

LIMITS: The extracts do not give the full text of Pai Foundation, Inamdar or Modern Dental College, and later treatment of all these judgments has not been checked.

relevant_law.summary: The right to establish and run an educational institution is an occupation protected by Article 19(1)(g). It is subject to reasonable restrictions in the public interest, which is the basis on which the State may regulate fees to prevent capitation fee and profiteering.

Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. As extracted in Islamic Academy [1], the essence of the guarantee is equal treatment: minority institutions are neither to be disfavoured nor favoured relative to majority institutions, and unaided minority institutions enjoy the same maximum autonomy as other private unaided institutions.

The law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. Among conflicting Supreme Court pronouncements, the larger bench and the later authoritative resolution prevail, which is decisive for the seat-sharing question. (Well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report.)

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The proposition that 'Section 309 IPC is unconstitutional' cannot be stated as the present law on the sources. The binding position is the contrary one. LAW: s. 309 IPC criminalised an attempt coupled with an act towards it [1]. For offences on or after 1 July 2024, BNS s. 226 applies, and it criminalises only an attempt made with intent to compel or restrain a public servant's official duty. COURT POSITION: Common Cause [4], a Constitution Bench, records at paras 36-38 that Gian Kaur held ss. 306 and 309 valid, that suicide involves positive overt acts not protected by Art. 21, and that the right to life does not include the right to die. It states that the legal position 'as of today' is that the right to life does not include the right to die. The Law Commission report [2][3] likewise records that the Supreme Court rejected the Art. 14 challenge, reasoning that varying gravity can be met by tailoring sentence and the Probation of Offenders Act. Under Art. 141, a Delhi High Court bench is bound by this; it cannot hold s. 309 unconstitutional. Whether the 2018 observations are ratio or restatement matters little, because Gian Kaur itself binds. The Law Commission report [5] is advisory only, not enacted law, and it expressly notes Gian Kaur dealt only with constitutionality, not wisdom. APPLICATION: For an offence committed before 1 July 2024, the charge is under s. 309 IPC, and a vires challenge fails on Gian Kaur; arguments must be directed to mitigation, probation, or absence of intent or of an act towards commission. For an offence committed on or after that date, s. 309 IPC has no application, and the prosecution must bring the case within BNS s. 226, which requires proof of intent to compel or restrain a public servant. An ordinary attempt without that intent is not an offence under s. 226. A continuing or mixed course of conduct should be analysed by date. The same BNS/BNSS dates-based rule governs procedure. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State would say Gian Kaur is binding and unreversed, that Common Cause [4] reaffirms it, and that Parliament's narrowing is a policy choice, not a concession of invalidity. What would defeat a challenge to s. 226 itself is the same reasoning, since coercion of a public servant has no connection with any claimed right to die. A petitioner would need a new ground, such as Art. 14 manifest arbitrariness or proportionality, which none of the sources decides. LIMITS: Gian Kaur is not among the sources and is known only through descriptions; no source addresses s. 226 BNS judicially; Rakesh Sharma [6] is irrelevant to vires. RISKS: citing the Bombay High Court view or the Law Commission report as law would be wrong. ADVICE: confirm the date of offence first; obtain the certified Gian Kaur report; argue mitigation or s. 226's intent element rather than unconstitutionality.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The advocate asks whether it is still good law that a Section 11(6) order is administrative. On the sources, it is not: the proposition is the position S.B.P. [2] rejected.

LAW AND COURT POSITION: Paras 23-24 of S.B.P. [2] record the earlier view, drawn from the line that Konkan Railway belonged to. On that view the Chief Justice's order was administrative, serving speedy constitution of the tribunal, not reviewable under Art 136 or Art 32, but challengeable in the High Court under Art 226, since the Act minimised court supervision. The Constitution Bench in para 46 [2] concluded at (i) that the power is not administrative but judicial, and at (xii) overruled Konkan Railway. Its ratio includes: delegation only to a judge of the High Court or Supreme Court (ii)-(iii); the designate decides preliminary aspects (iv); no district judge designation (v); appeal lies only under Art 136 (vii), with none against a CJI or designate order (viii); and the tribunal can decide Section 16 matters where constituted without recourse to Section 11(6) (ix). Conclusions (x)-(xi) are transitional and save past appointments. Under Art 141 and bench strength, S.B.P. binds the Bombay High Court. The Kerala, Jharkhand and Patna decisions [3][4][5] merely reproduce para 47 and carry persuasive weight only. Notably, [3], [4] and [5] quote the conclusions as para 47, whereas the Constitution Bench report in [2] numbers them para 46; the advocate should confirm the correct paragraph against the certified report.

APPLICATION: In Bombay, an order under Section 11(6) is to be treated as a judicial order made by the Chief Justice or a designated judge. A challenge lies by SLP under Art 136, not by writ under Art 226 or Art 32.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side may cite the administrative-order reasoning in [2] paras 23-24 and the object of minimal supervision. That reasoning is recorded in [2] as the view being departed from, and the overruling of Konkan Railway defeats it. The opponent might also point to later statutory change or later Supreme Court treatment. The sources do not cover amendments to Section 11 after 2005 or any later judgment on the nature of the power, and [1] reproduces the text only to sub-section (4). The extracts also do not show a Bombay High Court judgment.

RISKS: Reliance on a later-treatment-unchecked authority is hazardous, as the status line in each source says. Statutory amendment may have altered the scope of the Section 11 enquiry or the nature of the power, and I cannot say from the sources.

ADVICE: Cite S.B.P. [2] as binding. Do not argue the administrative characterisation. Verify subsequent treatment and amendments from the official law reports and the current bare Act.

precedents.holding_summary: The passages supplied reason that if both the exporting State and the delivery State could tax an inter-State sale despite Article 286(2), the transaction would bear double taxation compared with a local sale. They also reason that if neither State could tax, local trade would be disadvantaged against outside dealers. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is how the Explanation to Article 286(1)(a) is to be construed, and what United Motors [1] contributes. LAW: Article 286(1)(a) bars State taxation of sales or purchases outside the State. The Explanation deems a sale to occur where goods are delivered for consumption. Articles 286(2), 301 and 304 are read alongside. The text is not in the sources; obtain the Article as originally enacted and the present text, because the 1953 version was later amended and the current Article 286 differs. COURT POSITION: The passages supplied from United Motors [1] contain reasoning, not a stated operative holding. They reject two extreme readings. First, a reading allowing both exporting and delivery States to tax inter-State sales would impose double taxation and a discriminatory burden relative to local sales, which is what freedom of inter-State commerce seeks to avoid. Second, a reading under which neither State could tax would favour out-of-State goods over local goods, which is a perversion of that freedom. The Court's stated measure is that the delivery State taxes local and outside goods equally. Hurdut Roy [2] shows the case being applied to treat out-of-State sales as outside the Act. APPLICATION: Submissions available. (a) Construe the Explanation purposively, so that the delivery State is the State of taxation, avoiding double taxation. (b) Equal treatment: where the client is taxed in the delivery State, the tax must not exceed that on local sales. (c) If the client is taxed by a second State, argue discrimination and double burden under the reasoning quoted. (d) Use Hurdut Roy [2] for the proposition that transactions treated as outside the State fall outside the Act, and that exclusion differs from deduction. RISKS: The extract lacks the operative holding, so relying on it may mischaracterise the case. A bench may point out that Article 286 was amended, that the Explanation may no longer exist in that form, and that later Supreme Court rulings may have altered or overruled the position. The Orissa decision [3] concerns clause (1)(b), exports. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will say the passages are reasoning in support, not ratio; that the sales are within the State; and that the Explanation's deemed situs deliberately places the sale in the delivery State. PRACTICAL STEPS: Obtain the full text of United Motors [1] from the official report, confirm the operative order, check later Supreme Court treatment and Article 286 as amended, and map your facts onto the delivery-for-consumption test.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Golak Nath [1] and the Kesavananda opinions recorded in Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3] agree that Parliament's amending power is not unlimited and that judicial review of an amendment is not barred as a 'political question'. Sikri CJ, as recorded in [3], reasoned that the amending power cannot abrogate fundamental rights, which sits close to the Golak Nath result.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The core conflict is direct. Golak Nath [1] held that an amendment abridging fundamental rights is void under Art. 13(2). Kesavananda, as recorded in [3], overruled it and held that fundamental rights can be amended or abridged within the basic structure limit. Ray J., as recorded in [3], held the Golak Nath majority wrong and denied any implied limits. Golak Nath [1] itself left open whether the structure outside Part III is protected, which is the area Kesavananda later developed.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law moved from an absolute bar on abridging Part III (1967) to a power of amendment limited by the basic structure (1973). The notes also record the 24th Amendment (1971) and the 44th Amendment (1978), which put Art. 21 beyond suspension.

answer.conclusion: The proposition that Parliament has no power at all to amend fundamental rights was the holding of Golak Nath [1] but was overruled by Kesavananda Bharati, as recorded in Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3]. It cannot be put to the Madras High Court as current law, and doing so without disclosing the overruling would be unsafe. The workable submission is that amendments are justiciable [1], that the amending power is limited, and that an amendment abrogating a right forming part of the basic structure is void. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: You ask for a submission that Parliament has no power at all to amend fundamental rights, resting on Golak Nath [1]. The first thing to tell you plainly is that this proposition is not the law today and cannot be advanced as a statement of the current position. LAW AND COURT POSITION: The passages of Golak Nath [1] hold that the amending process is not a political question beyond review, that the amending power carries express and implied limitations, and that the Seventeenth Amendment, to the extent it abridges fundamental rights, is void under Art. 13(2). The Court expressly left undecided whether the structure of the Constitution outside Part III is protected, and whether the proviso to Art. 368 applies. Ashoka Kumar Thakur [3] records that the majority in Kesavananda Bharati overruled Golak Nath and held that fundamental rights can be amended, altered or abridged, with Sikri CJ, Shelat & Grover JJ. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] and Hegde & Mukherjee JJ. placing the limit at the basic features or identity of the Constitution. Under Art. 141, a Division Bench or single judge of the Madras High Court is bound by Kesavananda, a 13-judge bench, and cannot treat Golak Nath's core holding as binding. Passages in [1] cannot be confirmed from the record as the majority opinion, so any proposition from them should be attributed to the passage itself. APPLICATION: The honest and defensible way to use Golak Nath is as follows. (a) Submit that the reasoning on justiciability remains good: an amendment is open to judicial review and is not a political question [1], a point the later opinions in [3] share. (b) Submit that Parliament's amending power is limited, and that fundamental rights fall within the protected core to the extent they form part of the basic structure; cite Kesavananda as the binding authority and Golak Nath only as historical foundation. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] (c) If the impugned measure is an amendment abridging a particular right, argue the abrogation of that right destroys identity or a basic feature, relying on the Sikri CJ position in [3]. (d) Do not assert that Part III is wholly unamendable. A court may regard a submission that ignores this as lacking candour, which carries a professional risk. The State may also invoke the presumption of constitutionality. Which impugned amendment is in issue has not been stated, and I have not assumed it. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that Presidential satisfaction under Article 356 is beyond judicial scrutiny is not the present law. The real question is how far, and by what test, a court may review it.

LAW: Article 356(1) rests on the President's satisfaction, which under Article 74(1) is the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, as the Karnataka and Delhi High Court extracts of Samsher Singh and S.R. Bommai record [2][3]. Article 356(3) requires parliamentary approval.

COURT POSITION: The governing authority is S.R. Bommai (1994, nine judges), as applied by the five-judge Bench in In Re Article 370 (2023) [1]. The 2023 Bench states that it is bound by the S.R. Bommai majority on the reviewability of post-Proclamation action [1, para 197]. It holds that (i) the exercise of power after the Proclamation is subject to judicial review; (ii) it must have a reasonable nexus with the object of the Proclamation; (iii) the challenger must prima facie establish mala fide or extraneous exercise; and (iv) the onus then shifts to the Union to justify [1, para 514]. The same judgment records that the Proclamation itself is justiciable, and that if declared invalid the court may restore the status quo ante, revive a dissolved Assembly and Ministry, and validate action taken until then [1, para 98]. The standard of review is deliberately narrow: para 108, quoting S.R. Bommai, says the extent of power used is debatable and beyond judicially manageable standards unless 'so palpably irrational or mala fide as to invite judicial intervention', because of the 'political thicket' objection [1].

RATIO AND OBITER: The holding on reviewability and the burden-shifting test is ratio from the 2023 Bench [1]. The quoted passages from Sawant and Reddy JJ. are individual opinions in S.R. Bommai, as summarised in [1], not a single majority formula, and para 196 expressly notes the variation [1]. The Delhi High Court extract [3] only recounts those opinions and decides nothing.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The Union will say that satisfaction is a political judgment, that para 108 shows courts will not weigh the choice of measures, and that the 2023 decision upheld the Proclamation, granting wide latitude. Kaul J. said the President can make irreversible changes after parliamentary approval [1, para 98, para 112]. The answer is that these passages narrow the intensity of review and do not exclude it. The same opinions affirm justiciability and the burden shift.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: None of the sources reproduces the S.R. Bommai majority's own paragraphs on the grounds for challenging the initial Proclamation. Whether the 2023 decision addressed the pre-Proclamation material test is not shown in the extracts. The extracts relate to post-Proclamation action. Later treatment of [1] has not been checked.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Frame the challenge on specific material, mala fides or irrationality, to trigger the shift in burden.

relevant_law.summary: Empowers the President, on a Governor's report or otherwise, to issue a Proclamation where the State government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Clause (1) lets the President assume State functions and declare that Parliament will exercise the State Legislature's powers. Clause (3) requires parliamentary approval of the Proclamation.

The President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. Presidential 'satisfaction' is therefore the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, a point recorded in the Delhi High Court and Karnataka High Court extracts of S.R. Bommai and Samsher Singh [2][3].

The Supreme Court and High Courts can review a Proclamation by way of writ. The Madras High Court has jurisdiction under Article 226, but is bound by the Supreme Court's declaration of law under Article 141.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE. You ask whether a two-judge bench that followed the minority view in Bachan Singh can be treated as binding on the constitutionality of the death penalty and the rarest of rare test.

LAW. Under Art 141 the law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. Bachan Singh was decided by a Constitution Bench of five judges (4:1), and a two-judge bench is bound by it. The Chhattisgarh High Court's order [5], in a passage that records operative directions only, quotes Triveniben and Antulay for the proposition that a larger bench overrules or binds a smaller one, and that the court cannot skirt the larger bench's views. That passage is not itself a holding on this question, but the quoted rule is consistent with the Art 141 position in the constitutional notes (three judges cannot overrule five, Raghunath Rao). A fortiori, two judges cannot overrule five.

COURT POSITION. The sources consistently treat Bachan Singh as upholding the penalty. Panchhi [2] records that the Constitution Bench upheld the validity by majority and confined the penalty to the rarest of rare cases. The Panchhi extract carries a non-binding flag, so use it only as a description of Bachan Singh and not as authority in its own right. The 2022 order [3] rests its reasoning on the safeguards that justified upholding the penalty. The Delhi High Court [1] calls its approach a reassertion of Bachan Singh. None of these texts supports the minority view as law.

APPLICATION. If the 2-judge decision truly preferred the minority view, it cannot displace the majority holding. Such a decision would be per incuriam or an impermissible departure from a larger bench. The correct course for a coordinate or later bench is to follow Bachan Singh, or, if it doubts it, to refer the matter to a larger bench. You cannot cite that decision as binding authority on constitutionality or on the rarest of rare test. Which decision you mean is unclear to me. It may be that the bench only applied the minority's reasoning on a sentencing point, or that it expressed reservations obiter. You would need to read the actual ratio. If it merely applied the rarest of rare test, you can rely on it for that application but not for any attack on the majority.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The opposing side may say the bench was free to prefer the dissent on particular sentencing aspects, or that a later two-judge decision reflects evolving standards (for instance the fixed-term life sentences discussed in Surender [1]). The answer is that those developments operate within Bachan Singh and do not displace it.

LIMITS. Bachan Singh itself, its dissent and the 2-judge decision you describe are absent from the sources, so the point should be verified from the certified copies and the official law reports. I cannot confirm the decision's existence, bench strength or holding.

ADVICE. Do not rely on the decision as authority for constitutionality. Cite Bachan Singh and the cases applying it, and if you must use the decision, confine it to the narrow sentencing point actually decided.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The advocate wants Justice Ray's opinion cited as current binding law and confirmed as the Court's holding. The sources do not allow that, and I should not confirm it.

LAW: Under Article 141 the binding element of a multi-judgment decision is the ratio on which a majority agrees. A single judge's separate opinion binds only to the extent it forms part of that ratio. The sources record the Court's conclusion as follows: Article 368 carries inherent limitations, the power is large but limited, a limited power cannot be enlarged into an absolute one, and Parliament cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly [3]. The NJAC extract [4] describes this as the holding of the Kesavananda majority that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure. The Patna [1] and Gujarat [2] High Courts apply the same proposition.

COURT POSITION: None of the extracts attributes any of these propositions to Justice Ray or reproduces his opinion. The headnote passages in [3] are summary text and do not name the judge. The retrieved extracts also do not show how the nine-to-four or seven-to-six counting of the bench was done or who formed the majority. Citing Justice Ray as the source of the basic structure rule would risk mischaracterising the case, because the sources show only that the majority upheld the doctrine, and nothing here shows he was in it.

APPLICATION: The safe and accurate course is to cite Kesavananda Bharati (1973) [3] for the majority ratio, with the proposition drawn from the headnote at pp. 322 and 325-327, and to cite the NJAC judgment [4] and the Full Bench of the Patna High Court [1] as later applications. If Justice Ray's opinion is to be used at all, it should be identified by its page in the official report, and the advocate must establish from the report itself whether it concurred with, or was adverse to, the majority conclusion. Representing a separate or minority opinion as the Court's holding would expose the advocate to a serious adverse response from the bench.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side will say that an opinion cited as 'binding' that was not part of the majority ratio carries no Article 141 force, and that attributing the holding to a dissenting or differently reasoned judge is a misstatement of the case. That argument would be defeated only by pinpoint reference to the report showing his concurrence in the operative conclusion.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: None of the sources decides the content of Justice Ray's opinion, the final vote breakdown, or the Court's summary of views. Those must be verified from the certified official report.

ISSUE: The question is which provisions protect the identity of an 11-year-old rape victim and what they require of police and media.

LAW: The victim is a child under POCSO s. 2(d), so POCSO applies alongside the penal code. The substantive offence is IPC s. 376 if committed before 1 July 2024, or BNS s. 64 if on or after it; the date of the offence decides, and the query does not state it. POCSO may also be attracted for a penetrative offence, but the charge framing is not given. Procedure follows the date the proceeding began: if the investigation was pending before 1 July 2024 it continues under the CrPC; otherwise BNSS governs. The supplied material does not reproduce the text of the identity-disclosure offence under the penal code, nor POCSO s. 23, so those provisions must be verified from the official texts before filing.

COURT POSITION: Dongre [1] records that s. 24(5) POCSO requires the police officer to ensure the child's identity is protected from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest. The Court added that these provisions are for the victim's benefit and that a breach cannot be used to benefit the accused. This is a single-bench High Court view and, for Calcutta, only persuasive. Maroti Pimpalkar [2] is a Supreme Court decision binding under Art 141, but its extract concerns prompt reporting and the Act's object, not identity. Rameshwar [3] is unrelated to identity.

APPLICATION: For [NAME REDACTED], the police must keep her identity from the media, record her statement at her residence through a woman officer not below sub-inspector rank and not in uniform, and ensure no identifying detail (name, address, school, photograph) is released. Media is bound by the statutory restriction on publication; the precise offence and penalty must be confirmed from the statute text. The trial is before a Special Court under POCSO, with in-camera proceedings per s. 37 as noted above, and the Special Court may permit disclosure only in the child's interest.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The accused may argue that non-compliance with s. 24 vitiates the investigation or trial. Dongre [1] answers this, but it is only persuasive authority in Calcutta and was decided on its facts. The defence may also press the open-court principle; the response is the statutory in-camera mandate. Another risk is mis-selecting the code: charging under the wrong code because the offence date is unconfirmed.

ADVICE: Confirm the date of offence and the date the investigation began, check POCSO ss. 23, 24 and 37 and the penal-code disclosure offence against the Gazette text, and seek a Special Court direction on anonymisation of records and the order's title (using a pseudonym).

ISSUE: The question is which provisions cover cheating by personation committed online and where the complaint should be lodged, on a report made at Guwahati on 26 August 2026.

LAW: Two layers apply. (1) Substantive penal law: s. 66D of the IT Act [1] is directly on point, being cheating by personation through a communication device or computer resource (up to three years and fine up to one lakh rupees). Alongside it, s. 319 BNS (cheating by personation, up to five years or fine or both) applies if the offence was committed on or after 1 July 2024. If it was committed before that date, the corresponding IPC provision applies instead. The request does not state the date of the offence, and that date alone decides between IPC and BNS; the 26 August 2026 date is the date of the report, not of the offence. If the offence is a continuing one running across 1 July 2024, it is charged once under the BNS. General cheating (s. 318 BNS, with s. 318(4) as used in Deepak Kumar Jaiswal [4]) may be added where property was induced to be delivered, but the text of s. 318 is not before me and its elements must be checked from the statute. (2) Procedure: the proceeding began on 26 August 2026, so the BNSS applies, not the CrPC. The CrPC provisions in the [2]][3] are the repealed antecedents.

COURT POSITION: The Chhattisgarh orders [4][5] show how such cases proceed: FIRs combining BNS cheating with s. 66D, complaints from many States against one account, and strictness on bail and compromise. They are persuasive only in Assam. Inder Mohan Goswami [6], a Supreme Court decision binding under Article 141 (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report), requires dishonest intention at the time of the inducement, so the complaint must plead the deception and the inducement specifically.

APPLICATION ON JURISDICTION: Ordinarily an offence is tried where it was committed [2]. Where an offence results from an act and a consequence, it can be tried where either occurred [3]. BNSS s. 198 adds that where an offence is committed partly in one area and partly in another, or is continuing, any such area has jurisdiction. On the facts as stated, the informant reported at Guwahati. If the deception was received, or the money lost from the victim's account, in Guwahati, the consequence ensued there, so the Guwahati courts and police are a proper forum on the logic of [3] and s. 198 BNSS. The FIR or complaint should plead where the deceptive communication was received, where the transfer was made, and where the accused's accounts sit. The sources do not state the BNSS provision that replaces ss. 177 and 179, so its number should be verified against the BNSSs text.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The accused may argue that the offence was completed elsewhere (where the impersonator or the receiving account is), so Guwahati lacks territorial jurisdiction. The answer is the consequence limb [3] and s. 198 BNSS. The defence may also say the dispute is civil [6]; this is met by pleading dishonest intent from the outset. The sources do not decide whether a police station may register an FIR before jurisdiction is settled; none of the judgments cited here decides that point.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Plead the date, mode and place of each act; invoke s. 66D together with s. 319 BNS (or the IPC equivalent if the offence predates 1 July 2024), and s. 318 BNS if property was obtained. Preserve electronic evidence with the certificate required under the evidence law. Do not reproduce the informant's mobile and Aadhaar numbers in public filings without need.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question concerns the mode and the person for recording the statement of an 8-year-old complainant of sexual harassment of a child.

LAW: Two tracks operate. First, s. 24 POCSO [1] governs the police recording. The statement is to be taken at the child's residence, usual place of residence or place of choice, and as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below sub-inspector rank, who must not be in uniform. The investigating officer must ensure the child never comes into contact with the accused, the child cannot be kept at the police station overnight, and the child's identity must be protected from the media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest. Second, a Magistrate's recording. Under s. 183 BNSS (formerly s. 164 CrPC [2]), any Magistrate of the District where the information is registered may record the statement. Under s. 183(6)(a), for the listed BNS offences the Magistrate records the victim's statement as soon as the offence comes to police notice. It is recorded in the manner of s. 183(5), with the Magistrate empowered to administer an oath. As far as practicable, a woman Magistrate records it, failing which a male Magistrate in the presence of a woman. If the child is disabled, an interpreter or special educator assists and audio-video recording is required. The statutory text does not say that s. 183(6) applies to every POCSO offence; it lists specific BNS sections. Whether the facts here attract one of them must be checked against the FIR sections, and I do not state the content of those BNS sections from memory.

CODE: The date of the offence decides IPC or BNS. The date the proceeding began decides CrPC or BNSS: a proceeding pending before 1 July 2024 continues under the CrPC (s. 164), while an FIR lodged on or after that date follows the BNSS (s. 183), even for an earlier offence. These dates are not stated in the query.

COURT POSITION: Maroti Pimpalkar (2022) [3] emphasises prompt reporting and its link to medical examination under s. 27 POCSO, and states that medical evidence has corroborative value in sexual offences. It does not decide the recording of statements.

APPLICATION: For [NAME REDACTED], the police should record the statement through a woman sub-inspector or above, in plain clothes, at her home or a place she chooses, with no contact with the accused. Application to the Magistrate for a s. 183 recording should be made promptly if the offence falls within s. 183(6)(a).

RISKS/COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence may argue non-compliance with s. 24, such as a male officer, uniform, or recording at the police station. Section 24 uses 'as far as practicable' for the woman officer, so a lapse need not by itself vitiate the statement, but none of the judgments cited here decides the consequence of non-compliance. The prosecution may in turn contend that the Magistrate recording is independent of s. 24.

IDENTITY: The child's identity is protected under s. 24(5). The Aadhaar number given in the query is personal data and should not be reproduced in any filing, order or public record.

ADVICE: Verify the FIR sections, the dates, and the Chhattisgarh practice directions from the official records.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks for the limitation period for a s. 138 complaint where the cheque was returned unpaid on 11 November 2025. The answer depends on a chain of dates, not on the dishonour date alone.

LAW: Under s. 142(1)(b), the complaint must be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to s. 138 [2]. That cause of action arises only when the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receiving the demand notice [1]. The statutory chain is therefore: (i) presentation within six months of the date of the cheque or its validity, whichever is earlier, which is proviso (a); (ii) written demand notice within thirty days of receiving information of dishonour, which is proviso (b); (iii) expiry of fifteen days from receipt of notice without payment, which is proviso (c); (iv) a complaint within one month thereafter [1][2].

COURT POSITION: Narsingh Das Tapadia [4] holds that s. 142(1)(b) prescribes only the outer limit, and that a premature complaint is not fatal because cognizance, not filing, is the relevant act. Subodh Salaskar [6] holds that the court has no jurisdiction to take cognizance unless the conditions precedent are satisfied. Sainaba [3] holds that a notice sent by registered post to the correct address carries a rebuttable presumption of service, which fixes the date from which the fifteen days run. Subodh Kumar Rai [7] (Patna High Court, single judge, persuasive) holds that a second notice does not revive limitation and that a late complaint needs a sufficient-cause application.

APPLICATION: The 11 November 2025 date is only the dishonour date or the date of the bank's return. The thirty-day window for the demand notice runs from receipt of the bank's information, so the latest notice date should be calculated from the date the payee actually received the return memo, which is not stated. If notice is sent and received on day N, the cause of action arises on day N plus 15 and the complaint must be filed within one month from then. The request gives neither the notice date nor the date of its receipt, so no calendar date for the last day of filing can be fixed from the sources. Sudhakar [4]; Rajesh Kamat [5]). These are High Court decisions and bind only within their own States, so for Cuttack they are persuasive. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is which provisions cover online cheating by personation and where the complaint should be filed. LAW: Cheating by personation is defined in IPC s. 416 [1], reproduced as BNS s. 319 (punishment in s. 319(2): up to five years, or fine, or both). Section 66D of the IT Act [3] separately punishes cheating by personating by means of a communication device or computer resource, up to three years and fine up to one lakh rupees. Because the fraud is described as online, s. 66D is the natural primary provision, with s. 319 BNS (or s. 416 IPC with its punishment section) as the general overlap. CODE: The penal code cannot be fixed on this record. The offence date is not stated; 27 July 2026 is the date of reporting, not of the offence. If the personation occurred before 1 July 2024, the IPC applies, and if on or after it, the BNS. A continuing course of conduct across that date is charged once under the BNS. The proceeding began on 27 July 2026, so procedure follows the BNSS, with CrPC provisions cited only in brackets as repealed equivalents. FORUM: The general rule is CrPC s. 177 [2], which requires the offence to be tried where it was committed. In online fraud the act is often split: the deceptive communication is sent from one place, received in another, and money is delivered elsewhere. Section 198 BNSS permits inquiry or trial in any local area where part of the offence occurred, or where several acts were done in different areas. The complainant's Guwahati location suggests that the deception was received, or the loss suffered, there, which supports Guwahati as a place of trial, but the sources do not decide whether receipt of a deceptive message or loss of money is enough to locate the offence. No judgment is cited on that. The IT Act's own jurisdiction and investigation provisions are not among the sources, so I cannot state who may investigate s. 66D or the rank of the investigating officer. RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The accused may argue that the offence was committed wholly elsewhere, so the Guwahati court lacks jurisdiction, and that charging both s. 66D and s. 319 BNS [no such section: the BNS has sections 1 to 358] for one act is impermissible. The answer to the first is s. 198 BNSS (part-commission); the second requires authority that the sources do not supply. The record also does not show whether any personation, rather than plain cheating, actually occurred; the facts given are thin. The complainant's mobile and Aadhaar numbers appear in the query and should not be reproduced in the complaint or filings beyond what is necessary. answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is which provisions shield the identity of a 10-year-old complainant of sexual assault, and what is demanded of police and media. LAW: Under s. 2(d) POCSO the victim is a child, as Anurudh (2026) [4] stresses, so the child-protective regime applies. Section 74(1) of the JJ Act, 2015 [1] bars any media report on an inquiry, investigation or judicial procedure from disclosing name, address, school or any particular leading to identification of a child victim or witness, and bars publishing the picture. Section 74(3) [1] punishes breach with up to six months' imprisonment or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both. Section 74(2) [1] bars the police from disclosing the child's record. The POCSO direction quoted in Damodhar Dongre (2015) [2] requires the police officer to ensure the child's identity is protected from the public media unless the Special Court directs otherwise in the child's interest. COURT POSITION: Damodhar Dongre [2] is a single-bench Bombay decision and only persuasive in Rajasthan; the extract is operative and states no new proposition, though it clarifies that these safeguards are for the victim and a lapse cannot aid the accused. Anurudh [4] is an SC decision and binding, but it describes the legislative purpose rather than ruling on s. 74. APPLICATION: Police in Jaipur should keep the name, address, school and photograph of the child out of FIR copies, press briefings and any record released to third parties, and should not release the record for any certificate. Media must not publish anything leading to identification, including indirect particulars. Note that the query itself names the child; the name should not be repeated in pleadings that may become public, and a pseudonym should be used. The code question remains open: the offence date decides IPC (s. 376, BNS s. 64) versus BNS, and the date the proceeding began decides CrPC versus BNSS. RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A media house may argue that s. 74 speaks of a Board or Committee, and that its proviso does not fit a Special Court trial, so the section reaches only juvenile justice proceedings. The answer is the text: s. 74(1) expressly covers a child victim or witness of a crime under any other law; but no source decides this, so it must be checked. A second risk is that the Special Court, not the Board, may be the authority to lift protection. ADVICE: Seek a specific direction from the Special Court restraining disclosure, cite s. 74 [1] and the POCSO provision, and verify the statutory text and sub-section numbering from the official gazette and the reported judgments before relying on them.

relevant_law.summary: No report in any newspaper, magazine, news-sheet, audio-visual media or other form of communication on an inquiry, investigation or judicial procedure may disclose the name, address, school or any particular that may lead to identification of a child victim or witness of a crime, nor publish the child's picture. The proviso allows the Board or Committee holding the inquiry to permit disclosure, for reasons recorded in writing, in the child's best interest. precedents.holding_summary: The requirement to inform the arrestee of the grounds of arrest under Art 22(1) is mandatory in all offences, not a formality. Non-compliance violates Art 21 and renders the arrest illegal. Grounds must be furnished in writing, in a language the arrestee understands. The report records that ad interim bail was granted in the connected cases and that notice was issued to settle the issues.

precedents.case_name: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana & Anr.
precedents.holding_summary: Failure to inform the grounds of arrest as soon as may be vitiates the arrest, and the arrestee cannot remain in custody. Subsequent remand, chargesheet and cognizance do not cure it. Written grounds are the ideal course, though the court said there is no strict requirement of writing. The court left open whether re-arrest is possible.

precedents.case_name: Gobind Singh Gaida v. State of Uttarakhand
precedents.holding_summary: Compliance with Art 22(1) is decided on the record of each case. A signed arrest memo recording the grounds, with case diary entries, defeats the objection despite a loose answer in cross-examination. The court noted that Pankaj Bansal and Prabir Purkayastha arose under PMLA and UAPA where no arrest memo or written grounds existed. This is persuasive only outside Uttarakhand.

precedents.case_name: Sanjay Mukeshbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat
precedents.holding_summary: It recites the D.K. Basu guidelines: arrest memo attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee, informing a relative or friend, diary entry, medical examination. It treats the arrest memo as mandatory. Persuasive only in Jharkhand.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The client was arrested on 5 April 2025 in Ranchi for voluntarily causing hurt. The question is what rights attach to the arrest and whether bail can be sought. The PMLA material in the query does not apply to hurt, which is no scheduled money-laundering offence on these facts; the twin conditions of s. 45 PMLA are therefore not the governing bail test, and I would not argue them. LAW: Procedure follows the BNSS because the proceeding began on 5 April 2025, after 1 July 2024. The CrPC provisions [1][2] are cited only as the repealed equivalents. The penal code cannot be decided because the date of the offence has not been given. COURT POSITION: Art 22(1) and s. 47 BNSS (s. 50 CrPC [1]) require that grounds be communicated. Mihir Rajesh Shah [6] holds this is mandatory in all offences, that grounds must be in writing in a language the arrestee understands, and that breach makes the arrest illegal. Vihaan Kumar [3] adds that a vitiated arrest is not cured by remand, chargesheet or cognizance. Hurt is ordinarily bailable if simple, so s. 47(2) BNSS [1] also requires the officer to tell him he is entitled to bail and may arrange sureties. Production before a magistrate without unnecessary delay, within 24 hours, applies [2]. D.K. Basu guidelines on arrest memo, informing a relative, and medical examination [5] are also available, though Sanjay Mukeshbhai Patel [5] is only persuasive here. APPLICATION: The first step is to obtain the arrest memo, case diary entries and remand papers and check whether written grounds were served in a language the client understands, whether a relative was informed, and whether he was produced within 24 hours. Gobind Singh Gaida [4] shows that a signed arrest memo recording grounds will probably defeat this objection. BAIL: Whether the offence is bailable depends on its classification, which turns on the section actually charged (simple or grievous hurt, any weapon), and that is not stated. If bailable, bail is a matter of right and should be sought immediately before the police or Magistrate. If non-bailable, apply for regular bail under the BNSS, and consider s. 479 BNSS only if detention has reached the stated fraction of the maximum term. RISKS: Violation of Art 22(1) may not help if compliance is shown on record. A vitiated arrest may not bar re-arrest, which Vihaan Kumar [3] left undecided. Other pending cases would bar s. 479 relief. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will say the grounds were communicated and recorded in a signed memo, as in Gobind Singh Gaida [4], and that bail is a discretionary matter on the gravity of injury and risk to witnesses. ADVICE: Take instructions on the section charged, the injuries, prior cases, and the date of the offence. Do not argue the PMLA twin conditions.

precedents.case_name: Somappa v State of Karnataka (CRL.A/200068/2021)
precedents.holding_summary: The High Court upheld the conviction of a printer, editor and publisher of a fortnightly newspaper under s. 228A IPC and s. 23 POCSO for publishing material identifying a child victim. It held that the prohibition is mandatory and covers not only the name but any fact that makes the victim identifiable. It relied on Nipun Saxena (2019) 2 SCC 703, and the quoted passage of that decision is the source of the 'discernible identity' test. As a single-bench High Court decision it is persuasive only in Uttar Pradesh [3]. Its later treatment has not been checked.

precedents.case_name: Nipun Saxena v Union of India (as quoted in Somappa [3])
precedents.holding_summary: [UNVERIFIED — CONFIRM AGAINST THE OFFICIAL REPORT OR COURT RECORD BEFORE COURT USE] Reported in (2019) 2 SCC 703. As quoted in Somappa [3], the Supreme Court held that no person can print or publish the victim's name or disclose any facts that could lead to identification, and that blurring a face while showing relatives, neighbours or the village still discloses identity. It is binding under Art 141, but it is known here only through the extract in Somappa, and the full report should be read before it is cited (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report).

precedents.holding_summary: Under s. 44 UAPA and s. 17 NIA Act, a court may keep a witness's identity secret on recorded reasons, and the accused has a right of hearing on the application, though the identity stays undisclosed until orders are passed. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The victim is a 14-year-old girl in Kanpur and the charge is aggravated penetrative sexual assault. The question is which provisions shield her identity and what is demanded of police, media and the court.

LAW: Four layers apply. First, s. 228A IPC (BNS s. 72) penalises printing or publishing the name or any matter that may make the identity of a rape victim known [5][3]. Second, s. 23 POCSO, which Somappa [3] applied together with s. 228A, targets media disclosure of a child victim's identity. Its text is not in the sources and must be checked. Third, s. 74 JJ Act [1] bars any report on an inquiry, investigation or judicial procedure that discloses the name, address, school or other particular identifying a child victim or witness, and bars publishing her picture. Contravention carries up to six months, or a fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both. Section 74(2) also restrains the police from disclosing the child's records. Fourth, s. 327(2) and (3) CrPC [2] (BNSS s. 366) requires the trial to be in camera, as far as practicable before a woman Judge, and prohibits publishing proceedings without the Court's previous permission. Aggravated penetrative sexual assault under POCSO is not itself one of the offences listed in s. 327(2). The sources do not show that s. 327(2) covers a POCSO-only trial, though the same facts will ordinarily attract s. 376 IPC (BNS s. 64) as well, and POCSO's own in camera provisions should be checked.

COURT POSITION: Nipun Saxena as quoted in Somappa [3] holds that discernibility is the test. Naming the village, the school or relatives, or blurring only the face, can amount to disclosure. Somappa [3] upheld convictions of a printer, editor and publisher, and it is only a single-bench decision, persuasive in Uttar Pradesh. Premiya [5] records that courts should not name the victim in judgments even though judgments are exempt from s. 228A.

APPLICATION: The name '[NAME REDACTED]' in the query should not appear in any filing, FIR copy circulated outside the record, bail petition or order. Use 'the victim' or a pseudonym. Media may not publish her name, school, locality in Kanpur, family details or photograph. The police must not disclose her records or details outside the legal process, and the in camera trial should be requested at the outset. If an identifying publication occurs, the complainant may seek action under s. 228A IPC and the POCSO and JJ Act provisions, as in Somappa [3].

CODE POINTS: If the offence was committed before 1 July 2024, the IPC applies and the BNS number is only a cross-reference. If it was committed on or after that date, the BNS applies. For procedure, if the proceeding began before 1 July 2024 the CrPC continues under s. 531(2)(a) BNSS; otherwise the BNSS applies.

RISKS: The opposing side may argue that s. 74 JJ Act is confined to reports on JJ Act proceedings, or that disclosure was made in the public interest. The proviso to s. 74(1) lets the Board or Committee, not an ordinary criminal court, permit disclosure, so a media defence of authorisation must show a valid order. The exemption for High Court and Supreme Court judgments will not protect a newspaper.

ADVICE: Move the court for an in camera order and for anonymisation, and seek a direction against publication. Verify the full text of s. 23 POCSO, the BNSS/BNS numbers and Nipun Saxena from the official reports before citing.

The child's picture may not be published. The proviso lets the Board or Committee permit disclosure, for reasons recorded in writing, in the child's best interest. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks whether Section 365 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 applies to default bail. The premise appears defective. To my knowledge that Act has no Section 365, and none of the authorities supplied mentions it. Please confirm from the official text of the Act, since I cannot verify it from these sources.

LAW: Default bail does not arise from the arbitration statute at all. It arises from the proviso to s. 167(2) CrPC, now s. 187(3) BNSS, read with special-statute provisions such as s. 36-A(4) NDPS Act and s. 43-D(2)(b) UAPA. Sonu Kumar Saroj [1] and Nitish Kanda [3] both describe the right as arising under s. 167(2) CrPC (now s. 187 BNSS). Whether the CrPC or the BNSS governs a given case depends on the date the proceeding began (pending before 1 July 2024 under CrPC, begun on or after that date under BNSS); those dates are not stated in your query.

COURT POSITION: Bikramjit Singh [4] holds that the right is complete once an application is made on expiry of the period and before the charge sheet is filed, and that it forms part of Art. 21. Sonu Kumar Saroj [1] applies the principle to NDPS and holds that a later extension cannot retrospectively defeat an accrued right. Nitish Kanda [3] holds that the right is lost if not exercised before the challan. Hurba Petro [2] holds that an extension order is not appealable under s. 21 NIA Act, and that the remedy is review under s. 528 BNSS.

APPLICATION: An arbitration statute is a civil dispute-resolution framework and cannot govern a person's custody in a criminal case. Any argument that an arbitration provision affects default bail has no support in the sources. The counter-argument, that some provision of the Arbitration Act applies to bail, has no authority here and would fail for want of any statutory link.

RISKS: If you actually meant a different provision or Act, for example a section of the BNSS or of the NDPS or UAPA, the analysis would change. Citing a non-existent section in a pleading would damage credibility.

ADVICE: Verify the section reference, and if the real concern is default bail, frame it under s. 187(3) BNSS with the special statute, and file before the charge sheet.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The advocate asks whether s. 420 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies adultery as an offence. The premise is incorrect on two counts.

LAW: First, the 1996 Act is a civil, procedural statute. The sources show provisions on the arbitration agreement (s. 7) [2], ineligibility of arbitrators (s. 12(5)), termination of mandate (s. 14(1)(a)) and equal treatment (s. 18) in Cholamandalam [1], the time limit for awards (s. 29A) and challenge (s. 34) in the NHAI matter [3], and the self-contained, minimal-interference character of the Act in In Re Interplay (2023) [4]. Nothing in them creates a penal offence, and none shows a s. 420. I cannot confirm the full section list of the Act from these sources, but I am aware of no provision of the Act creating offences of this kind; please check the bare Act.

Second, s. 420 belongs to the Indian Penal Code and deals with cheating. Its BNS equivalent is s. 318. Adultery was IPC s. 497, which the Supreme Court struck down in Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018) (well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report). Adultery is therefore not a criminal offence under either provision. Whether it survives as a ground in civil or matrimonial law is a separate question under the relevant personal law and is not covered by the sources.

APPLICATION: If the advocate's concern is a cheating allegation, the code depends on the date of the offence: before 1 July 2024, IPC s. 420; on or after that date, BNS s. 318. Procedure follows the date the proceeding began, under BNSS or CrPC. If the concern is adultery, there is no criminal exposure after Joseph Shine.

RISKS/COUNTER-ARGUMENT: A party might argue that s. 420 IPC or BNS s. 318 could be invoked where a dispute that is also subject to arbitration involves deception. That is a separate criminal remedy. Whether the existence of an arbitration clause affects it is not decided by any source here, and I make no claim on it. Likewise, nothing in the sources shows adultery being used to found an arbitral claim.

Other punishment provisions of the Act (such as those for contravening s. 5 conditions on bigamy, which is cross-referred to the penal code) are not reproduced in the sources, so I cannot state them with confidence. 'Section 318' is, by the standard equivalents table, BNS s. 318, the successor of IPC s. 420 (cheating).
